script.opening: (On the phone, calm, polite, not wanting to bother anyone.) "Doctor, the sight in my right eye has gone funny over the last few hours — there were some flashes and little floaters earlier, and now it's like a grey curtain coming down over the side of it. The thing is, it doesn't hurt at all, so I figured it's probably nothing urgent and I could see how it goes over the weekend?"

facts.text: Flashes (like a camera flash at the edge of vision) and a shower of new black floaters started this morning, about 6 hours ago. The grey curtain began 2 hours ago.

"Yes, it's still there. The side of it is grey, like a shadow" — coming from the outer (temple) side and top. "I think it's creeping in a bit. The middle is still okay" — can read the clock with that eye. "It hasn't come back. It's been slowly coming across." Left eye normal.
"No, nothing like that" — no pain, no headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw pain on chewing, no weakness, numbness or speech problems, no double vision.
"No. I've just always been short-sighted" — strong glasses since childhood. No eye surgery, no injury. Last optician check 2 years ago.
"Only what's on my list for blood pressure, I'd need to check the names. Nobody's mentioned diabetes." (Amlodipine.) Not on blood thinners. No allergies.
Retired electrician, lives with his wife, Moira, who doesn't drive. His son lives 15 minutes away and could give a lift. Was planning to drive to his allotment.

Calm, polite, minimising because it doesn't hurt: "I didn't want to make a fuss when it doesn't hurt." If asked what he thinks: "Tired eyes, maybe." Then: "Well, you don't expect a curtain in your eye, do you." Surprised by urgency: "Today? Okay." and "Even without pain?" Agrees to go and to get a lift. If told it can wait, he will happily wait (the trap).

ice.ideas: "Tired eyes, maybe — it doesn't hurt, so it can't be serious."
ice.concerns: Doesn't want to make a fuss; quietly uneasy — "you don't expect a curtain in your eye".
ice.expectations: "To be told it can wait until after the weekend."

cues: "It doesn't hurt at all." — painless is not reassuring.
"Like a grey curtain." — retinal detachment story.
"I could see how it goes over the weekend." — needs firm, kind correction.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SUDDEN PAINLESS visual loss as an ophthalmic EMERGENCY — and that painlessness is irrelevant to urgency — rather than reassuring or deferring
Identifies the RETINAL DETACHMENT story (flashes + new floaters → curtain/shadow, especially in a myope) as time-critical for central vision
Screens the vascular differential — retinal artery occlusion (with GIANT CELL ARTERITIS screen in ≥50), retinal vein occlusion, and vitreous haemorrhage (diabetic/anticoagulated)

Establishes transient vs persistent — recognising transient monocular loss (amaurosis fugax) as a TIA needing urgent TIA-pathway assessment (NICE NG128: aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated; specialist assessment within 24 hours)

Takes a focused remote history (onset/speed, monocular, pattern, flashes/floaters, transient/persistent, GCA symptoms, vascular risk) and recognises the fundus cannot be examined remotely — arranging SAME-DAY emergency eye-service/ophthalmology assessment
Firmly but kindly corrects the "painless so it can wait" misconception without alarming the patient into disengagement, and conveys the urgency clearly
Explains the reasoning and checks understanding, ensuring the patient grasps why same-day assessment matters (sight is time-critical)

Safety-nets and arranges disposition: same-day emergency eye service today, advice not to drive himself (and that the DVLA Group 1 visual standard — number plate at 20 metres, 6/12 with both eyes open, field standard — applies after diagnosis), what to do if it worsens, and (for the older patient) GCA red flags needing immediate same-day steroid and eye review (BSR 2020) — emergency assessment, not wait-and-see

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang — but I have to be straight: the fact it doesn’t hurt doesn’t make it safe to wait. Sudden loss of vision in one eye is an eye emergency, and some causes need treating today to save the sight."

"The flashes and floaters, then a curtain coming across the side — that pattern, especially as you’re short-sighted, makes me think the retina at the back of the eye may be detaching. That’s time-critical."

"A few quick questions: is it just the one eye? Did the vision come back at all, or has it stayed? Any headache, scalp tenderness or jaw ache when chewing? Are you diabetic or on blood thinners? … That helps me know which emergency we’re dealing with."
"This needs to be seen today by the emergency eye service — not Monday, not the weekend. I’ll arrange that now; I can’t look at the back of your eye over the phone, and they can."

"Please don’t drive yourself — get a lift or we’ll sort transport. The eye team will tell you when it’s safe to drive again; there’s a legal eyesight standard for driving. Take your glasses and a list of your medicines."

"If it gets dramatically worse or you get severe pain, contact the eye unit straight away. Because of your age, a new bad headache, a tender scalp or jaw pain on chewing would need steroids and an eye check the same day, so ring us or the eye unit immediately. Weakness, a drooping face or trouble speaking — that’s 999. But the plan is: seen today. Okay?"

f.learning: Sudden PAINLESS visual loss is an ophthalmic EMERGENCY, and the dangerous trap is the patient’s assumption that "painless means it can wait" — the absence of pain is irrelevant to urgency. Triage the differential by the story. RETINAL DETACHMENT classically gives FLASHES (photopsia) and new FLOATERS followed by a CURTAIN/shadow progressing across the field, especially in a myope or after trauma/cataract surgery, and is time-critical because the chance of saving central vision falls once the macula detaches — so it needs SAME-DAY emergency eye-service assessment. RETINAL ARTERY occlusion causes sudden, profound, painless loss (a "stroke of the eye") and in those ≥50 mandates an active GIANT CELL ARTERITIS screen (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised ESR/CRP) because it threatens the other eye — suspected GCA with visual loss needs immediate glucocorticoid and same-day ophthalmology review (BSR, Mackie et al 2020); RETINAL VEIN occlusion and VITREOUS HAEMORRHAGE (especially in diabetic retinopathy or on anticoagulants) are other painless causes. TRANSIENT monocular loss that fully recovers is AMAUROSIS FUGAX — a TIA of the eye — needing urgent TIA-pathway assessment even after recovery (NICE NG128: aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated, specialist assessment within 24 hours). On the phone, take a focused history (onset/speed, monocular vs binocular, curtain vs central, flashes/floaters, transient vs persistent, GCA symptoms, vascular risk) and recognise that the fundus cannot be examined remotely, so sudden persistent visual loss with a detachment story warrants same-day emergency ophthalmology, never wait-and-see. Correct the painless=benign misconception firmly but kindly, arrange same-day assessment (College of Optometrists guidance), advise against self-driving (DVLA Group 1 visual standard applies after diagnosis), and safety-net (including GCA red flags in the older patient).

knowledge.guideline: [1] College of Optometrists Guidance for Professional Practice: flashes and floaters · [2] NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s (2019, updated 2022) · [3] BSR guideline for the management of giant cell arteritis (Mackie et al., Rheumatology 2020) · [4] Hollands et al., JAMA 2009;302:2243–9 · [5] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: visual disorders · [6] American Heart Association scientific statement on central retinal artery occlusion (Stroke 2021, international)
knowledge.summary: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye is an emergency whatever the pain level. Flashes and floaters followed by a curtain in a myopic eye is retinal detachment until an eye specialist has looked. Arrange same-day assessment, stop him driving, and screen for the vascular causes and giant cell arteritis.

points.t: Retinal detachment, retinal artery and vein occlusion, vitreous haemorrhage and ischaemic optic neuropathy are all painless. Urgency comes from sudden, persisting loss of vision, not from pain.

New flashes and floaters followed by a shadow or curtain spreading across the field in one eye suggests a retinal tear progressing to detachment. Myopia, previous cataract surgery and trauma raise the risk. In patients with acute posterior vitreous detachment symptoms, a subjective reduction in vision makes a retinal tear more likely (Hollands 2009 [4]). The College of Optometrists [1] sets out urgency by risk; a curtain or field loss needs same-day assessment by the eye service, because detachment spreading to the macula threatens central vision.

Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, profound, painless loss and is treated as a stroke equivalent (AHA 2021 [6], international). Retinal vein occlusion gives variable loss with vascular risk factors. Vitreous haemorrhage causes a sudden shower of floaters or haze, especially in diabetic retinopathy or with anticoagulation.

In anyone over 50 with sudden visual loss, ask about new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, systemic upset and polymyalgic symptoms. BSR 2020 [3]: suspected GCA with visual loss needs immediate glucocorticoid and same-day ophthalmology review.

Monocular loss that recovers fully within minutes (amaurosis fugax) is a TIA. NICE NG128 [2]: aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated, and specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset.

points.h: What a phone call can and cannot do
points.t: History can place the likely cause, but only a dilated fundal examination can confirm or exclude detachment. The safe disposition is a same-day slot with the emergency eye service, not a GP appointment on Monday.

He should not drive to hospital. After diagnosis, the eye team will advise on driving; DVLA [5] visual standards for Group 1 include reading a number plate at 20 metres and 6/12 acuity with both eyes open, plus a field standard.

Who can take him, whether he drives, what he was planning to do and why.

Retinal detachment versus retinal artery or vein occlusion, vitreous haemorrhage, GCA and amaurosis fugax.
Screened GCA symptoms and stroke features; asked about anticoagulants and diabetes.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

ro.d: Picked up “doesn’t hurt so it can wait” and the progression of the curtain.
Idea (tired eyes, painless means minor), concern (a curtain in his eye), expectation (to wait).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Aitken, it’s Dr Lewis returning your call. Can you tell me what’s happened?

The sight in my right eye has gone funny over the last few hours. There were some flashes and little floaters earlier, and now it’s like a grey curtain coming down over the side of it. It doesn’t hurt at all, so I figured it’s nothing urgent and I could see how it goes over the weekend.
Thank you, that’s a really clear description, and I’m glad you rang today. I need to ask some quick questions, because what you’re describing may need seeing today. Is that alright?
Today? Okay.
If you cover your left eye, what can you see with the right? Is the curtain still there now?
Yes, it’s still there. The side of it is grey, like a shadow.
Has it spread or got bigger since it started, and is the centre of your vision, like reading or faces, still clear?
I think it’s creeping in a bit. The middle is still okay.
Did the vision go suddenly all at once, or come and go at all?
model.why: Separates persistent loss from amaurosis fugax

model.text: It hasn’t come back. It’s been slowly coming across.
Any new headache, tenderness on your scalp when you brush your hair, or pain in your jaw when you chew? Any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking?
No, nothing like that.
Have you had any injury to the eye or eye surgery, such as cataract surgery?
No. I’ve just always been short-sighted.
And do you take any blood thinners, and have you been told you have diabetes?
Only what’s on my list for blood pressure, I’d need to check the names. Nobody’s mentioned diabetes.
You mentioned waiting for the weekend. What were you thinking it might be?
Tired eyes, maybe. I didn’t want to make a fuss when it doesn’t hurt.
I understand, and you’re not making a fuss at all. Is anything worrying you about it?
Well, you don’t expect a curtain in your eye, do you.

No, you don’t. Here’s what I think. The flashes and floaters followed by a curtain, in someone who is short-sighted, is the typical story of the retina, the seeing layer at the back of the eye, starting to come away. It doesn’t hurt, but it is an emergency.
model.why: Names likely retinal detachment in plain language

model.text: Even without pain?

Yes. Pain isn’t a good guide with eyes. The concern is that if it spreads to the centre, it can affect your reading and detailed vision permanently. Your centre is still clear, which is exactly why we should act today.
model.why: Corrects the misconception and links it to his own vision

model.text: Right. I see.

I’d like the emergency eye service to see you today. I’ll call them now, explain what’s happened and send over the details. They’ll look at the back of the eye with drops, which I can’t do over the phone.
model.why: Same-day eye service with direct handover

model.text: Please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who can take you, or would you like help arranging transport?
I can sort a lift.
Good. Take your glasses and your list of medicines. I’ll ring you back within the hour with where and when to go.

If before you’re seen the shadow spreads to the middle of your vision, the whole eye goes dark, or you get weakness, numbness or trouble speaking, call 999. If you get a new headache or jaw pain on chewing, tell the eye team straight away.
Can you tell me back what’s happening next?
You’re calling the eye unit, I’m going today with a lift, not driving, and 999 if it gets to the middle or I get stroke signs.
Perfect. I’ll call you back shortly, and I’ll check in after you’ve been seen.

social.t: Check he has a lift or arrange transport. Visual loss in one eye affects depth perception and safety on the roads.
Older patients often minimise symptoms. Thank him for calling and make clear that this is exactly what the practice is for.

legal.t: He must not drive today. After treatment, the eye team will advise; he must meet the DVLA Group 1 visual standards and tell DVLA if told they are not met or if both eyes are affected (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: Telephone assessment cannot examine the fundus; when a sight-threatening cause is likely, arrange face-to-face specialist assessment the same day and document the reasoning.
Speak directly to the eye service, send the clinical details, and arrange a callback so the plan does not rely on the patient alone (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Many areas have urgent eye care services through community optometrists, but a curtain or field loss should go directly to the hospital emergency eye service.

redFlags: Curtain or shadow across the field after flashes and floaters (retinal detachment)
Sudden profound loss (retinal artery occlusion, stroke equivalent)
Headache, scalp tenderness or jaw claudication over 50 (GCA)
Transient monocular loss (amaurosis fugax: TIA pathway)
psychosocial: Not wanting to make a fuss
ice: Idea: tired eyes; painless means not serious
Concern: “you don’t expect a curtain in your eye”
Expectation: to wait until after the weekend

playbook.diagnosis: “Flashes and floaters, then a curtain across your vision, in someone who is short-sighted, is the typical story of the retina starting to come away. It needs seeing today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The retina is like wallpaper lining the back of the eye. When it starts to peel, you see a curtain. The sooner it’s stuck back, the better the chance of keeping the centre of your vision.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought that because it doesn’t hurt it could wait. With eyes, pain isn’t a good guide, and this is one to act on today.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange a lift or transport, and make sure he knows where to go and when.
sharedPlan: Same-day emergency eye service; phone handover
Callback within the hour; follow-up after the eye review
safetyNet: 999 if the shadow reaches the centre, vision goes dark, or stroke symptoms
Report new headache or jaw pain on chewing to the eye team immediately
Contact the practice if he cannot get to the appointment

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is failed by being reassured by the patient. He tells you it is painless and can wait; the marks are for recognising a sight-threatening story, acting today and keeping him safe on the way.

items.why: Retinal detachment and vascular occlusions are painless. Delay risks the macula.
items.fix: Same-day emergency eye service, arranged by you.

items.fail: Not establishing whether the loss is persistent or transient.
items.why: Transient monocular loss is amaurosis fugax and follows the NICE NG128 TIA pathway.
items.fix: “Has the vision come back at all, even briefly?”

items.why: GCA can blind the other eye; BSR 2020 wants immediate steroids and same-day ophthalmology for visual loss.
items.fix: Ask about headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.

items.fail: Scolding him for wanting to wait.
items.why: He called because he was worried. Criticism makes him less likely to seek help next time.
items.fix: “I’m glad you rang today. Pain isn’t a good guide with eyes.”

items.fail: Leaving him to find the eye unit himself.
items.why: Patients get turned away or delayed without a handover.
items.fix: Call the eye service, send details, and ring him back with the time and place.

items.why: Monocular visual loss is unsafe for driving.
items.fix: “Please don’t drive. Can someone take you?”

items.why: “Call if worse” does not tell him what worse means.
items.fix: Name the triggers: spread to the centre, total darkness, stroke symptoms.

Cover test, persistent vs transient, spreading, centre spared or not, GCA and stroke symptoms, eye surgery or trauma, anticoagulants, diabetes.
“Tired eyes”, not wanting to fuss, waiting for the weekend.
Likely retinal detachment. Pain is not a guide. Same-day emergency eye service with a phone handover, no driving, callback.
999 for spread to the centre, total loss or stroke signs; GCA symptoms to report; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Accepts that it can wait because it is painless; books a routine appointment or suggests an optician next week; does not ask about transient loss or GCA; lets him drive.

Named likely retinal detachment in plain words and explained why painless does not mean safe.
Same-day emergency eye service with phone handover; told him not to drive; practical arrangements.
Hypertension and vascular risk noted; medicine list to take; follow-up after the eye review.
999 triggers named; GCA symptoms to report; teach-back; callback within the hour.

social.t: Check he has a lift or arrange transport. Visual loss in one eye affects depth perception and safety on the roads.
Older patients often minimise symptoms. Thank him for calling and make clear that this is exactly what the practice is for.

legal.t: He must not drive today. After treatment, the eye team will advise; he must meet the DVLA Group 1 visual standards and tell DVLA if told they are not met or if both eyes are affected (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: Telephone assessment cannot examine the fundus; when a sight-threatening cause is likely, arrange face-to-face specialist assessment the same day and document the reasoning.
Speak directly to the eye service, send the clinical details, and arrange a callback so the plan does not rely on the patient alone (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Many areas have urgent eye care services through community optometrists, but a curtain or field loss should go directly to the hospital emergency eye service.

redFlags: Curtain or shadow across the field after flashes and floaters (retinal detachment)
Sudden profound loss (retinal artery occlusion, stroke equivalent)
Headache, scalp tenderness or jaw claudication over 50 (GCA)
Transient monocular loss (amaurosis fugax: TIA pathway)
psychosocial: Not wanting to make a fuss
ice: Idea: tired eyes; painless means not serious
Concern: “you don’t expect a curtain in your eye”
Expectation: to wait until after the weekend

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Flashes and floaters, then a curtain across your vision, in someone who is short-sighted, is the typical story of the retina starting to come away. It needs seeing today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The retina is like wallpaper lining the back of the eye. When it starts to peel, you see a curtain. The sooner it’s stuck back, the better the chance of keeping the centre of your vision.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought that because it doesn’t hurt it could wait. With eyes, pain isn’t a good guide, and this is one to act on today.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange a lift or transport, and make sure he knows where to go and when.
sharedPlan: Same-day emergency eye service; phone handover
Callback within the hour; follow-up after the eye review
safetyNet: 999 if the shadow reaches the centre, vision goes dark, or stroke symptoms
Report new headache or jaw pain on chewing to the eye team immediately
Contact the practice if he cannot get to the appointment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is failed by being reassured by the patient. He tells you it is painless and can wait; the marks are for recognising a sight-threatening story, acting today and keeping him safe on the way.

items.why: Retinal detachment and vascular occlusions are painless. Delay risks the macula.
items.fix: Same-day emergency eye service, arranged by you.

items.fail: Not establishing whether the loss is persistent or transient.
items.why: Transient monocular loss is amaurosis fugax and follows the NICE NG128 TIA pathway.
items.fix: “Has the vision come back at all, even briefly?”

items.why: GCA can blind the other eye; BSR 2020 wants immediate steroids and same-day ophthalmology for visual loss.
items.fix: Ask about headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.

items.fail: Scolding him for wanting to wait.
items.why: He called because he was worried. Criticism makes him less likely to seek help next time.
items.fix: “I’m glad you rang today. Pain isn’t a good guide with eyes.”

items.fail: Leaving him to find the eye unit himself.
items.why: Patients get turned away or delayed without a handover.
items.fix: Call the eye service, send details, and ring him back with the time and place.

items.why: Monocular visual loss is unsafe for driving.
items.fix: “Please don’t drive. Can someone take you?”

items.why: “Call if worse” does not tell him what worse means.
items.fix: Name the triggers: spread to the centre, total darkness, stroke symptoms.
